answer: android.api is the targetSdk/target platform; android.sdk is the SDK platform buildozer installs and compiles against. For API 35 set both: android.api = 35 and android.sdk = 35, leaving minapi = 21 unless you must drop old devices. You also need buildozer/python-for-android new enough to know about 35, and SDK platform 35 plus build-tools installed. If you care about 16 KB pages, move to NDK r27 or newer, since r25b emits 4 KB aligned .so files. If Play rejects the upload, verify targetSdkVersion in the merged manifest, not just buildozer.ini. Google Play requires target 35 for new apps and updates from Aug 2025.

Do not follow either LLM suggestion; both are noise. window.gmo is created by Google's own ad snippets (Ads enhanced conversions, Ads data hub) injected by the gtag loader, so the errors come from third-party code running in users' browsers, not your bundle; 'invalid or unexpected token' is the same class of injected script. Your index.html is correct and needs no change. Note the comment says the tag is for Ads on Search only, so it does nothing in your React app: consider removing it. In Sentry, filter with beforeSend or ignoreErrors, dropping errors whose stack or URL contains googletagmanager.com, googleadservices.com or 'gmo'. Session Replay can tell you whether an extension or blocker triggers it.

The version string 'RELEASE' is not a real Maven version, so no repository can satisfy it. DBeaver's PostgreSQL driver definition shipped with jcenter() as a fallback, and jcenter was sunset in 2021 and shut down, so artifact resolution now fails. It is not the ODBC DSN or your network. Fix: in DBeaver open Edit Connection -> Driver Settings -> Libraries and set the driver version to a concrete number (for example 42.7.x) and switch Obtain driver from to Maven or Driver Manager, or delete the driver entry and let DBeaver download it again. Also clear cached artifacts under the DBeaver workspace maven repo and check Preferences -> Maven for a stale jcenter entry.

C++ has no such feature; the syntax you wrote is C#-like and invalid. An enum class enumerates values, not objects with fields. Idiomatic options: (1) enum class plus a constexpr lookup table of structs holding all codes and a find() that scans or binary searches; (2) drop the enum and use a struct Foo with static constexpr instances, which gives type safety plus multiple representations; (3) std::variant if you really want a sum type. For ISO 3166 a table of {alpha2, alpha3, numeric} plus an enum class CountryCode is the usual answer, with parse() doing the reverse lookup in both directions. Keep the magic numbers in exactly one table rather than scattered through compilation units, which is the real goal.

Note first that your snippet contains two copies of the same block and a bug in the else branch, which writes tx_buffer[0]='N' then immediately overwrites it with 'O'. For the repetition: compute one 16-bit opcode, for example uint16_t op = (rx_buffer[0]<<8) | rx_buffer[1], then use a switch, or better a constexpr table of {op, handler} pairs in a designated-initializer std::array and look it up, or an X-macro listing each command once and generating both the enum, the table and the handlers. A switch is the pragmatic answer: it compiles to a jump table, keeps each case independent, and the compiler warns about missing cases. Extract each command's behaviour into a small static function so every case is one line.

In C, NULL is commonly ((void*)0) and in C++ it is __null; it is not a typed const char*. In a variadic call only the default argument promotions apply, and the callee recovers values with va_arg using the type it expects. If the sentinel's actual type differs from what va_arg assumes, that va_arg call is undefined behaviour, which is what the analyzer reports. Casting to (const char *)0 is the portable, correct fix: it becomes a genuine null pointer constant of exactly the expected type, promotes to itself, and matches va_arg(const char *). Better still, replace the NULL sentinel with an explicit count, since a typed null cannot express end-of-list as safely. Do not silence varFuncNullUB without the cast.

The exception is thrown by Google Play services because it cannot verify which package is calling. In practice it means the API key's package restriction does not match your real applicationId, or the SHA-1 of the signing certificate is not registered. Two common causes: the manifest has an applicationIdSuffix (.debug/.staging) and you registered the base id, or you rebuilt with a different signing key. Check the Cloud Console credentials for the Android key, confirm the package name and the SHA-1/SHA-256 of your upload key (keytool -list -v -keystore ...), then reinstall a clean build. Also confirm the API_KEY meta-data entry is inside the application tag of AndroidManifest and that com.google.android.gms is a declared dependency. Installing SDK tools cannot fix a key mismatch.

VS Code 1.97 added a built-in SVG preview, so the change is not yours. Force the text editor instead: add a file association, for example 'files.associations': { '*.svg': 'xml' }, which makes SVG open as markup; or pin the editor per file with 'workbench.editorAssociations': { '*.svg': 'xml' } or default_editor. Also open Settings and search svg to see the new preview-related toggles the release added, and check the Extensions tab for an update to an SVG/image preview extension that may now claim .svg. Update to the newest 1.97.x patch as well, since preview behaviour was adjusted in patch releases.

There is no corruption; printf simply reads the argument area sequentially. On i386 every variadic argument is passed as a 4-byte slot, so your 8-byte long long is consumed as two slots. With the wrong specifier %lx, printf reads only the low half, 0x22222222, and the next %x then reads the remaining upper half, 0x11111111, which is why the second value looks wrong too. A single mismatched specifier silently desynchronizes everything after it, and passing a mismatched type is undefined behaviour. Always compile with -Wall -Wextra -Wformat=2 and use inttypes.h PRIx64, which prints correct specifiers on 32- and 64-bit builds.

Your model is missing one category: an expression evaluates either to a value (rvalue) or to an lvalue, which designates an object. a as an lvalue designates a; the read that turns it into 5 is the lvalue-to-rvalue conversion. Similarly *(ptr+1) is an lvalue designating arr[1]. Evaluating it produces the designation, not a value, and that is the only thing assignment's left operand needs: it must know which object to store into. For a simple variable the designation is implicit; for *(ptr+1) you must evaluate to get the address, so &*(ptr+1) == ptr+1. In your notation, evaluation yields either a value or a designation, and assignment converts the LHS designation into a location plus a store, with the result being the stored value.

Tailwind v4 is configured in CSS, not JS: there is no tailwind.config.js unless you ask for one. Put settings in the stylesheet, for example @import 'tailwindcss'; then @theme { --breakpoint-xl: 80rem; } for breakpoints, and for container-like behaviour either write your own with @utility container { margin-inline: auto; width: 100%; max-width: var(--container-xl); } or just use mx-auto plus a max-w-* utility. For custom component classes with responsive and hover variants, define them in a @layer components block and use @apply md:flex hover:text-slate-500 inside, which keeps variants working. Arbitrary variants (md:, hover:) work on any class you author yourself.

The _UIReparentingView warning is emitted by UIKit itself when a popover/hosting view is inserted under the hosting controller; it comes from the new iOS 26 Menu presentation path, not from your code. The visible glitch is a rendering regression in 26.x. Workarounds to try: replace Menu with MenuPicker (iOS 17+), which uses a different code path; or drive a plain popover with .popover or a custom sheet; or drop the unnecessary ZStack and VStack nesting around the Menu. If you can isolate a minimal case, file it with Feedback Assistant, since only Apple can fix the animation.

The failure is in downloading PhantomJS, not in Selenium or your site. RSelenium's rsDriver tries to fetch the phantomjs binary from the Bitbucket repository ariya/phantomjs, which Bitbucket removed, so the HTTP call fails (402/404) and rsDriver aborts before Chrome starts. Fixes: install PhantomJS yourself so RSelenium finds it on PATH (npm install -g phantomjs-prebuilt), or stop using rsDriver and drive Chrome with chromote, or use RSelenium with a chromedriver you installed via wdman. If you only need Chrome, calling rsDriver(browser='chrome') without chromever and with your own chromedriver avoids the phantomjs code path entirely.

Your own stylesheet is loaded after Tailwind's, and some of your selectors are more specific than the utilities, so you are overriding them. nav.container (class plus element) beats p-6 (single class), .navbar a beats space-x-6's margin utility, and .btn-nav with padding-block/padding-inline overrides py-2/px-6 because your sheet comes last. The universal reset * {margin:0;padding:0} is not needed, since Tailwind v4 already ships preflight. Remove the hand-written rules, or move them into Tailwind's cascade with @layer components/base inside your CSS entry so utilities win, or express them as @utility so they participate in variants and ordering.

Yes, via the Keyboard Shortcuts editor: Ctrl+K Ctrl+S, search chat, and find the view commands such as View: Toggle Chat (workbench.action.toggle.chat) or View: Open Chat (workbench.action.chat.open), then assign a chord. Recent versions ship Ctrl+Alt+I / Cmd+Alt+I for chat. If nothing appears, the Copilot Chat extension may not be installed or enabled, in which case the commands are absent: install or enable GitHub Copilot Chat and reload the window. You can also write the binding directly in keybindings.json, and use View: Reset View Locations to recover the layout after dragging the panel to zero width.

This is inherent, not a missing update. An associative container only requires operator<, so the tree must navigate with less-than: at each node it compares and picks left or right, and an equal result must be resolved by descending left and continuing. Hence equal comparisons repeat: you compare 8 with 8, go left, compare 7 with 8, then compare 8 with 8 again. The implementation-independent way to express find/contains is a lower_bound followed by an equality check, so you pay at most one extra comparison per lookup, and a three-way operator<=> cannot remove it because the container requirement is still operator<. C++20 set::contains only avoids forming an iterator; it does not change the comparison count.

Bruno does have script output, just not as an always-visible Postman-style panel. Open the Console tab next to Tests/Docs in the request window (View: Toggle Console, or the Console button in the tab bar) and run the request again; output from pre-request and post-response scripts appears there, and script errors are reported there too. Make sure scripting is enabled in Settings and that you executed the request after adding the log. In Bruno CLI the same output goes to the terminal, and in the VS Code extension it appears in the extension's output channel. If the tab is missing, update Bruno, since the console has been reworked across 1.x releases.

The extra translucent strip is added by the system, not by your toolbar: in iOS 26 the input container between inputView and inputAccessoryView is drawn with the new Liquid Glass material, and it appears when both a custom inputView and a custom inputAccessoryView are set. There is no public API to remove that container background. The practical fix is to stop using UIToolbar as the accessory: build a plain UIView containing a Done UIButton, set its backgroundColor to .clear or .systemBackground as needed, and assign that as inputAccessoryView. Keep the button's configuration colors explicit rather than relying on tint inheritance, and size the view yourself.

These are editor and tooling complaints, not Tailwind errors. VS Code's built-in CSS service does not know Tailwind's v4 at-rules; install or update the Tailwind CSS IntelliSense extension, or set 'css.lint.unknownAtRules': 'ignore' in VS Code settings to silence it. If Tailwind is actually failing to build, the usual cause is still using the old PostCSS plugin: in v4 you must use @tailwindcss/postcss in postcss.config (or the @tailwindcss/vite plugin), and @import 'tailwindcss' replaces the three @tailwind directives. Verify by running the dev server and inspecting the emitted CSS for utility classes; if they are present, only your editor is unhappy.

Several reasons. First, llvm-mca's push model is pessimistic; the dependency you see is on rsp, but push is not on the critical path of the values being saved, so that chain is not real latency. Second, push is one byte of encoding versus four or five for mov with a displacement, which matters for icache and code size in cold code. Third, mov requires a separate sub rsp: an extra uop that every later stack access depends on, and it complicates variable-size frames, alloca, shrink-wrapping and unwinding. Compilers do switch away from push when the target model says it is slow, which is why Darwin targets use mov plus str for x86-64. Your measurement is real, but it omits the matching pops.

Gemini 1.5 Flash has been retired from the API, so the model id no longer resolves and you get 404; quota problems return 429 and API version mismatch is not the cause. List what you can use by iterating genai.list_models() and filtering for generateContent support, then move to a current 2.x Flash or Pro id and update the code plus any stored model name. The SSL errors are unrelated: WRONG_VERSION_NUMBER and BAD_RECORD_MAC mean something answered a TLS handshake with plain HTTP, typically a corporate proxy or a bad HTTPS_PROXY setting. Check HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and any MITM certificate. The Flask server binding to local HTTP is fine and has nothing to do with either issue.

Two things. First, the result is only repeatable because srand(time(NULL)) is seeded once per second, so reruns within the same second give the same sequence; that is determinism, not accuracy. Second, with n=10000 the standard error is about 0.045, so a value consistently near 3.25 means real bias, not luck. Note printf with %f given an int is undefined behaviour and misprints your coordinates: use %d and drop the per-point printing. With x,y uniform on [-10000,10000] and radius 10000 the circle is inscribed in the sampled square, so the expected inside fraction is pi/4 and the x4 factor is correct; print min/max of x and y and the count d to confirm the sampling spans the full range.

Your find directive is wrong: config is itself a package directory, not a folder containing packages, and where must list roots. Use a flat layout where the project root holds the packages, for example [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ['.'] include = ['config*','packages*'] with a matching package-dir, or a src layout where = ['packages/src'] and move config under packages/src. Also note that a top-level module named config is a bad global name likely to collide with other packages. A cleaner option is hatchling with [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] packages = ['config','packages/src'], or a single src/ layout, and renaming config to yourapp.config. Finally, uv pip install -e . only helps if you run the script with that interpreter.

The library is telling the truth about the value it received, so that value is not the 13-character password you logged. Most likely you are hashing a wrapper object or something else entirely (a token, a pre-hashed value, serialized bytes), so inspect type() and len() of the exact object passed to the hash/verify call inside the deployed app, not the variable you think you pass. Another possibility is a passlib/bcrypt version mismatch where the backend behaves differently in the container than locally. Never work around it by truncating to 72 bytes, since that silently weakens every password. Fix the value being passed, and consider the bcrypt_sha256 scheme if you must support long passphrases.

Turn it off in Tools: Options. For the suggestion list, open Tools -> Options -> Text Editor -> IntelliSense and uncheck Enable IntelliSense (or, for C++, set Enable IntelliSense to Disabled under Text Editor -> C/C++ -> Advanced). Copilot has its own page, Tools -> Options -> GitHub Copilot, with checkboxes to turn off completions and chat; otherwise uninstall the GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot Chat extensions from Extensions -> Installed and restart Visual Studio. To disable Copilot fully for the machine, turn off both the Options checkboxes and remove the extensions, since Copilot also contributes the whole-document completion you are seeing.

The error says require was used, so Vite is loading your config as CommonJS. Tailwind's Vite plugin is ESM only, hence the message. Fix it by telling Node the project is ESM: add 'type': 'module' to package.json, or rename vite.config.js to vite.config.mjs (Vite 6 also supports .mts). Verify there is no leftover require in the config and that nothing makes Node treat .js as CJS. If a stale cache is suspected, delete node_modules/.vite and reinstall. Also make sure the package.json you deploy to GitHub Pages actually carries the type field.

PlaceAutocompleteElement is a custom element with its own shadow DOM, so ordinary descendant selectors cannot reach the inner input. The supported hook is CSS parts: style place-autocomplete-element::part(input), ::part(placeholder), ::part(matched-substring), ::part(icon) and ::part(clear-button), plus the host itself with a normal class. Set background, border, border-radius, padding and font on the input part to match your form and control layout on the host. Check the current Maps JavaScript reference for the exact part names supported by the API version you load, since they have changed. If you need full control, keep your own input and open the element in a popup, or fall back to the legacy Autocomplete widget, which is freely styleable but deprecated.

That error means the package NuGet handed you has no DotnetToolSettings.xml, so the CLI cannot treat it as a tool; it is not a broken install on your side. It usually comes from a stale or mirrored NuGet source serving a non-tool package under that id, or a partially cached download. First run dotnet nuget list source and remove any internal mirror, then run dotnet nuget locals all --clear and dotnet tool uninstall --global dotnet-ef. Install a version matching your target framework explicitly, for example dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef --version 8.*. A cleaner setup for a repository is a local tool manifest: dotnet new tool-manifest, then dotnet tool install dotnet-ef, which pins the version for everyone.

Arthenica retired ffmpeg-kit and the released artifacts were pulled from Maven Central, so no repository in your list can satisfy the coordinate. Drop jcenter() from repositories, since it is long dead. Realistic options: use a community-maintained fork that publishes the same API to Maven Central (the API is unchanged, so only the group id moves), publish the archived source to your own internal Maven repository, or replace the dependency. For playback/transcoding on Android the usual replacement is AndroidX Media3 Transformer, or drop the native library entirely and drive a bundled ffmpeg/ffprobe binary through ProcessBuilder, which is what most surviving forks now do. Clean and refresh Gradle caches after changing coordinates.

These are transient intermediate artifacts created by MSBuild's BuildHost targets, which spin up small net472/netcore host projects for legacy designers and design-time builds (WPF/WinForms designer or the Visual Studio design-time build). They are regenerated on demand and are safe to delete; nothing at runtime or publish depends on them. They normally live under obj, so if they appear at the project root a tool or an older build configuration put them there: delete them and keep obj ignored. If they end up inside your publish output, check that your publish item globs are not picking up the project root, and clean obj and bin before republishing. Checking git status for the exact paths will confirm where they came from.

The size is not stored anywhere at runtime. The standard requires nothing about representation; in practice the compiler evaluates the size expression once, emits the stack-pointer adjustment (sub rsp, size, with realignment if needed) and, at scope exit, emits the matching adjustment using a size it computed at compile time. If the size expression has side effects the compiler keeps its value in a hidden stack slot, which is an implementation detail, not a language feature. That is why sizeof on a VLA type is itself an expression evaluated at run time and only valid inside the declaring scope, and why a pointer to a VLA cannot tell you its length. alloca behaves the same way: nothing records the size, so you must keep it yourself.

This is an iOS 26 behaviour change: bar items now live in the new glass bar environment, and the bar applies its own tint to custom views, overriding what you set on them. tintColor inheritance for a custom view is documented as unreliable, and 26 makes that more pronounced. Stop relying on inherited tint and set colors directly on the content: build the button with UIButton.Configuration and set baseForegroundColor, or use a UIImage with withTintColor and renderingMode .alwaysTemplate, set the segmented control's selectedSegmentTintColor and its title text attribute foreground color, and use UISwitch's stateful setter setThumbTintColor(_:for: .off) if you need the thumb. tintColor on UIBarButtonItem(customView:) or on the navigation bar is not a supported way to color a custom view.

langchain 1.0 removed the legacy langchain.chains API, so langchain.chains no longer exists in that package; this is expected, not an install problem. Also, langchain-community 0.4.x with langchain 1.0.5 is not a supported pairing. Choose one: if you want the old tutorial code, pin langchain==0.3.x with matching langchain-community, text-splitters and Vertex AI integration versions and keep create_retrieval_chain; if you want 1.0, migrate to the new API, wrapping retrieval as a tool and using create_agent, following the langchain 1.x migration guide since the class-based chains moved out of the main package. Verify with python -c 'import langchain; print(langchain.__version__)' inside the same environment uv created.

That is a deprecation warning from the AGP DSL inspection in Android Studio, not an error; your project still builds and produces the same manifest. AGP has been renaming these accessors over the years (compileSdkVersion to compileSdk in AGP 7), and newer AGP versions deprecate older spellings in favour of the newer property surface, so a strikethrough on the Groovy accessor in 8.12 is that deprecation, not a reversal. Hover the word to read the exact replacement AGP suggests and check the AGP 8.12 release notes for the DSL migration; if you want to stay put, keep whichever spelling AGP now prefers or suppress the inspection. Semantically nothing changes: compileSdk selects the API you compile against, targetSdk is the behaviour level you opt into.

That message means the native side asked AppRegistry for a component literally named auth, which matches the app's registered name rather than anything you pass to registerComponent. So your index.js is either missing registerRootComponent(App), or it does not import the App you think it does, or app.json/package.json name is auth while nothing registers. Check that index.js does import { registerRootComponent } from 'expo', imports App from './App', and calls registerRootComponent(App), that main points at index.js, and that expo.name/slug in app.json match your project. Renaming files and clearing Metro caches can never fix a name or registration mismatch; also confirm nobody registers a component called auth.

That text is PyCharm's message for indexing a type alias that takes no template arguments, and in this snippet there is no alias at all, which means the name it thinks it is subscripting has been shadowed. Most likely something called list (or List, or a name used in an annotation) is defined as a TypeAlias or in a stub, so PyCharm resolves the built-in list to your alias and complains when you index it. Hover the reported name to see where the alias comes from and check the project and site-packages for a TypeAlias assignment or a .pyi stub. Since the code runs, this is inspection-only. Fix the shadowing, or avoid indexing entirely with f-string unpacking such as f'... {", ".join(invitation_list)}'.

As of the C++26 cycle nothing from the safety-profiles direction has been merged: no adopted subset, profile switch or checked mode. P3081 set the direction and profiles were named as the likely vehicle for investment, but the proposals that would yield adoptable features (bounds annotations, checked containers, restricted downcasts) have not landed, and there is active opposition in the committee, so nobody can promise C++26 or C++29 content. Expect incremental opt-in work: annotations, constexpr-friendly checks, better static diagnostics and library-level safe abstractions, none of which give dynamic memory safety. Track the WG21 paper list and P3081's status pages for real movement, and treat blog or LLM claims of safe C++ in C++26 as unverified.

Both do something, but different things. const int bar makes the member itself const: through any non-const foo object you may read it but never assign it, and in C it also makes the whole struct non-assignable, so you must initialise it. const int *bar is a pointer to const int: the pointer is mutable, the pointed-to int is not modifiable through it. In C++ the first form is almost always a mistake, because a const data member deletes the implicitly-declared copy and move assignment operators, so foo becomes non-assignable and awkward in containers; use a private member plus accessors or a getter returning const int& instead. Use the second form when you want read-only access to someone else's data.

There is no std::ranges facility that zips N ranges into a struct, but with C++23 it is short: pipe std::views::zip(vec1, vec2, vec3) through std::views::transform with a lambda unpacking std::get<0..2>(t) into MyData, then into std::ranges::to<std::vector>(). zip_view is C++23, so on C++20 fall back to std::transform over an index range built from std::views::iota, indexing each vector with the same int, and reserve the output first. Your loop is already fine; just use size_t instead of int. If the struct keeps gaining fields, consider storing std::array<std::string,3> so the zip needs no per-field unpacking, or generate the transform body with a macro.

Two faults chained: a general protection fault becomes an unhandled double fault, then a triple fault, which resets the machine. The log shows the real cause: fetch_raw_descriptor with an index above the GDT limit, so the selector you load does not exist in your GDT. enter_user_mode loads 0x23 and pushes 0x1b as CS, so entries for those selectors (indices 4 and 3) must exist with the correct limit, base and DPL 3. Also note push 0x800000 is a 20-bit immediate in 32-bit mode: verify that address is mapped and marked present and user, that a TSS supplies ESP0 for the CPL change, and that cli before iret is not leaving user code with interrupts disabled.

The rule exists because a virtual function's identity must not depend on template arguments: for a given dynamic type, the vtable must have an entry for every function the base declares. If a derived class could constrain its override, the override would silently vanish for some instantiations while calls through Base* still had to dispatch, so the call would reach a base function with a different contract, and final-overrider lookup breaks. It also breaks template argument deduction. The supported pattern is the one you found: constrain the class template (partial specialization, or a requires clause on the class), or provide unconditional overloads that delegate with if constexpr, or use CRTP so dispatch never relies on the virtual table.

The reference documentation shipped alongside the feature: search the Visual Studio documentation (learn.microsoft.com) for slnx, which has a New, simpler solution file section describing enabling it, migrating with dotnet sln migrate, and an element/attribute reference, plus the dotnet CLI docs for dotnet sln. The schema itself is implemented in the Microsoft.VisualStudio.SolutionPersistence library in the dotnet/extensions repository, where the README and the source that defines valid elements and attributes are the authoritative answer to your questions. Note the format was preview in the first VS release that supported it and stabilised later, so check the docs version matching your VS/SDK, and note the element set is still small, with unknown elements rejected rather than ignored.

vb.X is a minified identifier in code Google serves to your web app, so this is a Google-side or injected third-party failure, not your Apps Script code and not something a redeploy of your code can fix. The pattern (works after a refresh, fails across unrelated apps, starts on a given morning) points at a bad or partially rolled-out client bundle, an A/B experiment, or an extension or ad blocker injecting conflicting globals. Things to try: hard reload and clear cache, test in a private window with extensions disabled, and check whether the deployment is still set to execute as the owner rather than execute as the accessing user. Capture the HAR and a console trace with timestamps so Google can correlate. As a workaround, roll back to the previous deployment version if the breakage followed a deployment.

You cannot make parts of a value alias other variables; C++ gives no way for a uint64_t to be a window onto two uint32_t objects. Pick one representation as the source of truth. Option A: keep the uint64_t and expose lo() and hi() with shifts and masks, or add setters. Option B: make the two halves the real storage, struct Pair { uint32_t lo, hi; }, and convert with std::bit_cast<std::uint64_t>(p) in C++20 (well-defined) or memcpy for older code. Option C, if the halves come from hardware or another thread, keep a single std::atomic<uint64_t> and change it with fetch_add or a compare_exchange loop, never with unsynchronised halves. Note that 0u may be unsigned int, so cast carefully and prefer uint32_t.

Two separate requirements must both hold, and per-library warnings can clear while the APK-level warning remains. The .so files must be linked with 16 KB-compatible page alignment (NDK r27 or newer, or an explicit -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384), and the APK must store them uncompressed and zip-aligned to 16384 so the loader can map them directly. Set android.useLegacyPackaging=false with AGP 8.5.1 or newer and confirm the merged manifest carries that value. Verify with the APK Analyzer alignment check and zipalign -c -P 16 -v 4 on the final APK, and confirm every native library, including transitive ones, is 16 KB aligned; the build machine's page size does not matter.

You are hitting the PEP 639 transition, which needs recent tooling. license = {text=...} and license = {file=...} are deprecated, and license = 'MIT' only works with setuptools 77 or newer; the unrecognized or malformed field 'license-file' error means the metadata version you produced and your twine/build do not agree, so upgrade build, setuptools and twine together. Then write license = 'MIT' as an SPDX expression plus license-files = ['LICENSE'], and delete any License :: classifiers, which PEP 639 forbids alongside an SPDX license. Run python -m build and inspect METADATA in the wheel to confirm Metadata-Version 2.4 before uploading.

That line comes from AppOps in system_server, not from your app, and it is a log, not an error. On Android 15/16 AppOps verifies the attribution source of media calls; when playback starts outside a visible Activity it cannot tie the call to a declared component and logs this. Check where your MediaPlayer.create runs: do it from an Activity or a proper foreground service rather than an application context or a background receiver. If it runs in a service, declare FOREGROUND_SERVICE and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK, start the service correctly, and set a media session or attribution source if you use MediaController. Filter with logcat -s AppOps:E and only worry if audio actually fails; no manifest tag just silences it.

In Tailwind v4 the tailwindcss package no longer ships a CLI binary, so npx has nothing to run; the CLI moved to @tailwindcss/cli. Install it with npm i -D @tailwindcss/cli and run npx @tailwindcss/cli init -p. Better still, you need neither a CLI nor a config file in v4: add @tailwindcss/postcss to postcss.config (or use the @tailwindcss/vite plugin) and put @import 'tailwindcss'; in your CSS, and the framework auto-detects your sources. If you genuinely need the legacy v3 setup, install tailwindcss@3 and run npx tailwindcss@3 init -p.

In constant evaluation there is only the thread doing the evaluation, so no other thread can notify, and blocking would deadlock the compiler. The C++26 wording is written on that premise: these operations must not block during constant evaluation, so a wait that would block is treated as returning immediately, effectively a spurious wake. Practical consequences: never write a constexpr function whose progress depends on wait unblocking, and treat the atomic's value as the only meaningful state. I would verify the exact wording for your toolchain against [atomics.types.operations] as amended, since the phrasing has been revised during the C++26 process and a stricter implementation may diagnose rather than return.

ts(2882) is the TypeScript diagnostic for a side-effect import of a module it cannot resolve types for, and for CSS that resolution depends on the ambient declarations Next.js generates in next-env.d.ts. If that file was deleted or excluded from tsconfig, every CSS import errors at once, which matches the symptom of nothing in your code having changed. Fix: run npx next dev or next build once to regenerate next-env.d.ts, make sure tsconfig.json includes it and that it is not gitignored, and confirm VS Code uses the workspace TypeScript (TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version -> Use Workspace Version). If it persists, a newer TS or Volar release tightened the check; silence it per line or through typescript.semanticValidationRules until you update Next.js.

That is a stale lock file or a case-insensitive ref collision. Git creates ref.lock files while updating and removes them afterwards; if a git process crashed, or antivirus, an indexer or OneDrive grabbed the file, the lock survives and every fetch fails identically. Close all git processes (taskkill /F /IM git.exe), then delete the offending .lock files under .git/refs/remotes/origin and any stale .git/packed-refs.lock, and exclude .git from AV scanning. If the lock does not exist or reappears immediately, suspect case-colliding branch names: on NTFS Foo and foo are the same path, so git cannot create the second ref and reports File exists. Find them with git for-each-ref refs/remotes/origin and rename one side, or fetch from WSL/Linux where refs are case-sensitive.

Do not pin an exact patch in requires-python. uv init --python copied your argument straight into the project, giving requires-python = '==3.9.21', which makes uv look for that exact interpreter and then fall back to a system one it finds. Use a range instead: requires-python = '>=3.9,<3.10' or ~=3.9. Then install and select the patch version explicitly with uv python install 3.9.21 and uv python pin 3.9.21, which writes .python-version, and run uv sync --python 3.9.21. Check uv python list to confirm the managed interpreter is discovered, and watch for UV_PYTHON or a python-preference setting overriding discovery. Reinitialising with uv init --package --python 3.9.21 sandbox after deleting the directory also works.

Rust returns by value because ownership makes it the safe default: the callee constructs the value and transfers ownership, so aliasing is impossible and there is nothing for an out parameter to buy you. The performance worry does not apply: building a value directly into the destination the caller already owns is exactly the case compilers elide, so there is usually no copy at all. There is no named-return-value-optimization guarantee in Rust, but out parameters would force a caller-provided buffer or a &mut plus a length, which is worse. Rule of thumb: return by value, and if a profile ever shows a large copy, restructure so the callee writes into caller-owned storage, for example filling a caller-provided Vec.

The node binary downloaded fine; only the npm step failed, because nvm-windows extracts npm into a temporary folder and something deletes or blocks it before it is read. Common causes: Defender or another AV quarantines the temp files, the %TEMP% path is inaccessible or too long, or you are not elevated. Run nvm install from an elevated prompt, add the temp directory and NVM_HOME to Defender exclusions, then delete leftover nvm-install-* and nvm-npm-* folders and retry. If it still fails, bypass the npm step: download node-v14.17.3-win-x64.zip yourself, extract it to %NVM_HOME%\v14.17.3, and run nvm use 14.17.3. For old Node versions generally, nvm for Linux/WSL, fnm or n avoid the problem because they unpack official archives.

Yes, but do not hand-write a parallel C struct. Safe pattern: define the storage type once in a header usable from both languages, or keep the template in C++ and expose only functions. Concretely, put template struct Queue in queue.hpp, write explicit instantiations (template struct Queue<int, 8>;) in queue.cpp so the members are emitted, and add extern 'C' wrappers such as bool qint8_push_back(Qint8*, int) that call the specialization. If C needs to embed or size the object, expose opaque handles plus a size query (size_t Qint8_size(void)), or use the C-compatible layout struct as the member storage and let the template wrap it, so there is exactly one definition of the layout. Duplicating the struct in C risks padding and alignment mismatches.

std::format is not constexpr in C++23, and it cannot become so while returning std::string, since constructing a string needs heap allocation, which a constant expression forbids. The formatting core was made constant-evaluable for C++26, so with a C++26 compiler you can use std::format_to or std::format_to_n into a fixed-size std::array<char, N> using a constexpr-friendly output iterator inside a constexpr function, then return the array. On C++23 the practical answer is std::to_chars, which is constexpr and produces the same digits, or a hand-written constexpr formatter. If you need a NUL-terminated result, expose a std::string_view over the constexpr array.

Same failure mode as the other nvm-windows report: Node 14 downloaded, npm 6.14.18 did not, because nvm-windows stages npm in a temp folder and the file goes missing or is blocked. Clearing temp folders will not help. Run the install from an elevated command prompt, exclude the temp directory and NVM_HOME from Windows Defender, and retry after deleting any partial v14.21.3 folder. If it persists, install that version manually: download node-v14.21.3-win-x64.zip, extract it to %NVM_HOME%\v14.21.3, then run nvm use 14.21.3. For old Node versions generally, nvm for Linux/WSL, fnm or n avoid the problem because they unpack official archives directly. Setting NVM_HOME, NVM_SYMLINK and TEMP to short paths without spaces also fixes it in some setups.

R's vectors concatenate, so you need to interleave explicitly. The shortest answer is as.vector(rbind(vec, paste0(vec, '.1'))): rbind makes a two-row matrix and as.vector reads it column-major, giving x, x.1, y, y.1, z, z.1. Equally explicit: paste0(rep(vec, each = 2), rep(c('', '.1'), times = length(vec))). A base-R loop works too: unlist(lapply(vec, function(x) c(x, paste0(x, '.1'))), use.names = FALSE). The rep(each = 2) plus a repeated suffix vector is usually clearest if the suffix may later vary per element.

printf and wprintf are different streams with different encodings. printf converts narrow characters using the CRT's current output code page, which SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) changed, so it worked. wprintf does not consult SetConsoleOutputCP; on Windows the wide CRT functions use the stream's text mode, which defaults to _O_TEXT and mangles the surrogate pair. Set the mode explicitly before any output: include <fcntl.h> and call _setmode(_fileno(stdout), _O_U16TEXT), or _O_U8TEXT for UTF-8. Call it before writing anything to stdout, and do not mix printf and wprintf on the same stream, since orientation is fixed on first use. The console also needs a font containing the glyph, and Git Bash/MSYS terminals do not support this.

Your reading is right: declaring an implicit intent filter with ACTION_MAIN (and, in practice, CATEGORY_LAUNCHER) makes almost every installed app visible to you under Android 11+ package visibility filtering. It is not QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES: no permission is involved, and you see only what the query returns. Google Play policy still applies: broad queries must be justified as core functionality (a launcher, a default-handler or share-target chooser, automation, backup), and Play scrutinises MAIN/LAUNCHER declarations; using the queries mechanism to enumerate apps without a legitimate core feature is a policy violation even without the permission. Declare specific packages with a package element or a narrower intent with a specific action, category or data scheme, and keep the Play Console declaration in sync.
